why: Name the actor: 'The LLM knows the design...' gives a concrete subject, and the subject-first order reads faster than A's passive-leaning 'is known to the LLM'.
Only a synonym and word-order change ('largest' vs 'biggest', 'If stuck' vs 'If you are stuck'); no taste rule or past call separates them.
A's 'Request a plan from it first' is the tighter wording; B's added 'First ... it' is an extra orienting word (shorter wins, fewer words read faster), though the difference is marginal.
'plausible answer' is more neutral and precise than 'believable answer'; 'When a line is blank' is equivalent to B, so the difference is slight.
B's 'When in doubt, check before uploading it' swaps a plain clause for a longer one with no added information; A is shorter and clearer, with no rule favoring B.

'Join clues that sit in different places' is a literal act the student can picture, while 'combine clues stored apart' is more abstract; this follows 'a metaphor for a literal act becomes the literal act'.
B is shorter and keeps a plain imperative; A's 'watch for' adds nothing and both are otherwise equal, so little rule separates them. Marginal: shorter wins.
'has no files' vs 'without any files' is a wording preference; no rule or past call separates them.
Plain 'Split ... side by side' is more concrete and literal than 'Divide... in parallel'; 'parallel' is a mild jargon, but difference is small, so lean on concrete picture over abstraction.
'Separate an agent that does two jobs' is plainer and clearer than 'Divide an agent handling two jobs'; concrete subject, everyday word.
Wording-only variant of the same sentence; no taste rule or past call separates them.
Same claim in different words, same length; no rule or past call clearly favors either.
Names the actor and uses a concrete subject ('The report contains…'); B's passive 'is found in the report' is wordier and weaker.

'Narrow it far enough and the system is both safe and useless' vs 'Scope it down far enough and the system ends up safe and useless': both are equivalent wording with no rule or past call separating them.
Only 'back everything the claim states' vs 'support all that the claim says' differs; no rule or past call separates them.
'compare it with my work contract' vs 'verify it against my employment contract' is a near-synonym swap. B's 'verify' is a more precise act, but that is not a clear rule-based win.
Both are wording variants of one sentence at the same length; neither follows a rule or past call that the other breaks.
Shorter: it drops the 'When you ask... it gives' clause and keeps the claim ('Fewer words read faster').

B is plainer and shorter, with a concrete subject-free phrasing ('Any later run... begins from'); A's 'The following run, whatever the topic, starts with' is wordier and slightly claude-speak. Minor, but shorter wins.
'permit the agent to hit send' vs 'let the agent press send' differ only in wording; both repeat the lead-in and neither breaks a named rule.
Names the actor: 'this judge passes it' with a concrete subject; A's 'lets it pass' is looser and 'Even a grounded claim' leans toward clever; difference is small.
'That will not work' vs 'This does not work' is a wording difference; neither follows or breaks a rule or past call.

A's 'is not up against nothing' is a plain-word contrast that fits the slide's frame; B's 'does not compete with nothing' then 'competing with that' repeats the verb and reads clumsier, but the difference is small, so it is closer to same.
B names the actor and gives the student control ('Every candidate you pick should name how it moves...'); A's 'Each picked candidate should state' is passive and abstract (name-the-actor rule).
Only 'has to keep it running... when it goes wrong' vs 'must keep... when it is wrong'; no taste rule or past call separates them.

'Name attached to it... does not move inside a folder' is plainer and literal; A's 'has a name on it... travel' is a looser metaphor and B fits the 'literal act over metaphor' and 'metaphor must fit its noun' cuts.
Only difference is 'In Module 6, the SHA check was that rule' vs 'The SHA check from Module 6 was that rule'; no taste rule or past call separates them.
'objects; revises' vs 'disagrees; redrafts' are equivalent in meaning and length; neither breaks a taste rule or past call.
Differs only in 'With no sponsor present'/'labels' vs 'Lacking the sponsor'/'marks'; neither follows a rule the other breaks.
Only the clause order differs; both state the same fact in the same number of words and neither follows a rule the other breaks.
